chapter_theme: Akananuru 121 to 140, from the மணிமிடைபவளம் section: paalai partings argued with the heart or comforted by the friend, kurinji night-tryst poems spoken for an overhearing lover (the sleepless town, the dangerous path, the mother's Murugu rite), three mullai returns in the rains, a neythal pair of men smitten by a girl's eyes, and a full wedding night recalled in marutham, with puram fame (Karikal at Vaakai, Anni and Thithiyan, Cheralathan, Kazhuvul's Kamur, Thithan's Uranthai) used as the scale of comparison.

121.reading: The man tells his heart they have cause for joy: the girl of broad soft shoulders, they say, will come with him into the summer forest of black-faced langurs, where a bull elephant washes his young mate's head with the muddy water of a dug pit in a shrunken pond and rests in the striped shade of a kadamba, and where a startled beast calls to a traveller's white rice-bundle blown by the wind, taking it for its mate.
121.nuance: The road is shown at its worst (the shrunken pond, the travellers killed by Mazhavar raiders, their food parcels blowing loose), so the joy of the first line is the measure of what she is willing to cross with him. The beast that mistakes a dead man's rice-bundle for its mate turns the image of companionship into one of loss.

colophon.thurai: தோழியால் தலைமகளை உடன்வருமெனக் கேட்ட தலைமகன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: she is to leave home with him across the dry land, the parting of udanpokku

occasion.words: தோழியால் தலைமகளை உடன்வருமெனக் கேட்ட தலைமகன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

iraicchi.act: in the drought the bull elephant washes his young mate's head and rests with her in the shade
iraicchi.sense: as the tusker tends his mate on the parched road, so the man will tend the girl who crosses it with him

122.reading: With her lover listening outside, the girl tells her friend that their secret love has as many hindrances as the old stony outskirts of Thithan's Uranthai: the noisy town never sleeps, and when it does the mother does not, then the watchmen, the young spearmen, the dog, the bright moon, the owl at the ghost-hour and the cock each keep watch in turn, and on the one night when all are asleep he does not come.
122.nuance: The poem is a chain: each sleeper hands the watch to the next, and the last link is the lover's own absence, so the complaint aimed at the overhearing man is that he is the final obstacle. The listing presses him toward marriage without saying so.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொற்றது. தோழி சொல்லெடுப்பத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the obstacles to a night meeting in secret love

comparisons.tenor: the full moon's light
their secret love, beset on every side

occasion.words: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொற்றது

123.reading: In the middle of the desert the man rebukes his heart: you cannot cross the hills where elephants, gaunt like fasting ascetics, file along narrow paths and bring back wealth, yet if you stay embracing her you fear poverty; like the tide at the Chola's Kaveri mouth that comes in with prawns and goes out with garlands, you hold to neither, so be ruined.
123.nuance: The tide image is exact: the heart neither goes nor stays but swings between the two each day. The elephants likened to ascetics who neither eat nor bathe make the road itself a place of renunciation.

thinai_evidence.note: the man torn on the road between going on for wealth and turning back

comparisons.tenor: the starving elephants filing along the path
the gleam of the Chola spear-blades
the Chola army's many shields
the heart that swings between going and staying

124.reading: The man, his campaign ending, tells the charioteer that if the enemy bring tribute and elephants and bow and ask the king to go, the king's army will enter today; so, to end the camp's hardship and gladden their beloved in the mansion, he must drive the swift horses with harness like lightning down the long road fragrant with rain-opened mullai, scattering the bees, and reach by morning the walled town where the evening drum sounds.
124.nuance: The man's homecoming waits on the enemy's surrender: the puram event decides the akam one, and he plans the drive before the tribute has even come.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-opened mullai along the road of return

comparisons.tenor: the gold-wrought harness of the horses

125.reading: Addressing the north wind, the speaker says that while he is away for wealth, and the rain-clouds that have emptied themselves roam the sky like an elephant past its must, the wind torments the lonely in the cold midnight; but if the man gone on his worthy work comes back soon, the wind will flee like the nine kings without honour who left their nine umbrellas at midday on the Vaakai field before great Karikal.
125.nuance: The colophon gives the friend speaking to the heroine on hearing he has returned, but the poem itself is spoken to the wind in the first person plural (எமக்கே), and the return is still conditional (வல்வரின்). The defeated kings are made a measure of disgrace: the wind will run as they ran.

colophon.thurai: 2தலைமகன் வினைமுற்றி மீண்டமை யுணர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்கச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting through the rains for the man gone on his work

comparisons.tenor: the ripe buds of the eengai
the white eengai flowers strewn about
the dark kuvalai buds
the cloud that has poured and is empty
the north wind put to flight

126.reading: The man tells his heart, which will not stop following the young girl with a parrot's prattle, kayal eyes, cloud-dark hair and lightning waist, that besides its own long sorrow it may perish like Anni, who would not be held back by the kind counsel of Evvi, lord of a rich Kaveri land where a bard's daughter refuses old paddy for the vaalai fish her brothers caught by night and takes pearls instead, and who fought Thithiyan for his punnai tree.
126.nuance: The Anni story is a warning of ruin from obstinate desire, and Evvi's rejected counsel stands for the advice the heart will not take. Nothing in the poem fixes whether the girl is a wife in sulking (alternative 1 of the colophon) or a girl not yet won (alternatives 2 and 3).

colophon.thurai: (1) உணர்ப்புவயின் வாரா ஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது. (2) அல்ல குறிப்பட் டழிந்ததுமாம். (3) தோழியைப் பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: river, vaalai fish and paddy of the watered land, though they belong to the Evvi simile

comparisons.tenor: the pearls the bard's daughter receives
the heart that may perish for its desire
the girl's small prattling speech
her large painted eyes
her dark hair falling down her back

occasion.words: உணர்ப்புவயின் வாரா ஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது
தோழியைப் பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்

127.reading: The friend comforts the wasting girl: even if in a single day he could win treasure like the hoard of tribute that Cheralathan, who drove off the sea-foe, cut the kadamba and carved his bow on the Himalaya, heaped at Maanthai and left for the earth to eat, he would not stay a day longer in that land of strange speech where bowmen crowned with kadamba wait at the forks of the road.
127.nuance: The argument runs by scale: the largest wealth the hearers know, a king's buried tribute, would not hold him one extra day, so he will surely come. The kadamba appears twice, once as the enemy's guardian tree that Cheralathan felled and once as the wild bowmen's crown.

thinai_evidence.note: the dangerous forks of the road in a land of another tongue

comparisons.tenor: the wealth he might win in a single day

128.reading: With her lover outside, the girl tells her friend that the village has fallen silent and midnight comes on cruel as a killer, and her love overflows its banks like a sea; why then does her heart, without consulting either of them, go out tonight to the narrow path over the rocks, narrow as the rope on an elephant's back, slippery with rain and full of hidden pits, to watch his steps and hold up his faltering feet as he comes wearing kuvalai from the mountain spring?
128.nuance: The fear is turned around: the girl is anxious not for herself but for him on the night path, and since he is listening, the danger she describes is the argument for ending the night meetings by marriage.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்ததலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகள்தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain path at midnight

comparisons.tenor: the cruelty of the midnight hour
the narrow path along the rock ridge

129.reading: The friend tells the girl that the man who shared her trembling nights and said one must keep her in mind after parting cannot forget her, for, his heart opening, he said that the hard desert, where a stag calls its doe to rice fallen from the bamboo, where in a ruined border hamlet a bird feeds its mate young cotton bolls and poor women gather the burst seed, and where raiders who ate fat cattle crowd the clear spring, would not be hard to cross with her.
129.nuance: Two creatures feed their mates in his description of the road (the stag calling its doe to food, the bird feeding its mate), and the friend sets them before the girl as his own words. The quotation marks of the base text are unclear at lines 1 and 3, so which words are the man's and which the friend's is not fixed.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard dry track with its raiders

iraicchi.act: the bird feeds young cotton bolls to its mate in the ruined hamlet
iraicchi.sense: the man who noticed a bird feeding its mate on that road will not forget to care for the girl

130.reading: The man answers the friends who rebuke him: had you seen her face to face you would not rebuke me, for the bold look of that young woman's bright face, her painted eyes that put to shame the bee-opened neythal of the curving backwater, at the harbour of Korkai of chariot-lord Vazhuthi, where thaazhai guards its white flowers and horses' hooves crush the pearls the waves bring in.
130.nuance: The whole shore of Korkai is laid out as the setting of a single look: the pearls trodden underfoot by horses tell how rich the place is, and the girl's eyes defeat even the flowers of such a shore.

thinai_evidence.note: the screw-pine, the neythal flower and the sandy shore

comparisons.tenor: her painted eyes, which the flowers turn their backs to

131.reading: The man refuses his heart, which says that giving is worth more than the girl with bee-dark hanging hair and a cool garland, and bids him come through the dread forest where the hero-stones of men who died recovering cattle driven off at dawn by bowmen, crowned with peacock feathers and inscribed with name and fame, stand along every path like a hostile front of planted spears and shields: I will not come, heart; may your work succeed.
131.nuance: The heart argues from a puram value (ஈதல், the giving that needs wealth), and the man answers with the price of that value, the hero-stones of men killed on the road. The dismissal, வாய்க்கநின் வினையே, turns the usual blessing on the departing man into an ironic farewell to his own heart.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot dread track lined with hero-stones

comparisons.tenor: her dark hanging hair
the rows of hero-stones along the path

132.reading: Meeting the lover after leading the girl home, the friend tells him that the millet is harvested, the girl's forehead has lost its beauty to lovesickness and the town eyes her and talks; so if he loves this hunters' sister with bamboo shoulders and rain-cool eyes, let him take her away to his own town walled by great hills, where a small-winged bee that opened the buds by the spring sips the vengai, sleeps in the honeyed kaanthal and dreams of the elephant's must.
132.nuance: The harvest of the millet ends the daytime meetings in the field, which is why the friend speaks now. A traditional reading takes the bee that moves from vengai to kaanthal as a hint at the lover; the poem gives only one correspondence, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: millet, vengai and kaanthal of the hills

133.reading: The girl tells her worried friend that he once asked her, in vain, whether she could come with him to drink the wind-blown spray of a flower-laden forest stream in a rain-fresh pasture land of vengai, kaayaa and ilavam where white clouds drift like bow-beaten cotton; now he has crossed alone the wild Milai track where a twisted-horned stag keeps his young doe that chews the marul grass.
133.nuance: The remembered invitation is all mullai freshness, the present road is paalai; she sets the land he offered her against the one he took alone. The colophon says she means to show she can bear it, but கொன் ('in vain') carries a reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the forest without her

comparisons.tenor: the white rat's red eyes
the white clouds drifting
the dark kaayaa blossoms
the red ilavam flowers
the ripe vetchi buds

iraicchi.act: the stag keeps beside its young doe as she grazes
iraicchi.sense: even the stag of that forest stays with its mate, yet he crossed it without her

134.reading: Returning with his work done, the man tells the charioteer that the rains have come and the forest is lovely, with sapphire-blue poovai, red velvet-mites and fallen mullai on red soil like a master's painting; let the horses step softly and forget the goad, for if the twisted-horned stag and his doe in their loving union hear the swift chariot, [they will be parted], and still a midnight meeting can be theirs at home.
134.nuance: The man spares the mating deer the noise of his chariot on his way to his own reunion; his care for them is the tenderness he brings home. The syntax of the last two lines is compressed, and whose union the midnight meeting is (the deer's restored, or his with his wife) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest pasture in the rains

comparisons.tenor: the blue poovai flowers
the red-soil pasture strewn with flowers
the stag's twisted horns

iraicchi.act: the stag and doe lie together in loving union
iraicchi.sense: the deer's union is the one the man is hurrying home to, and the care he takes not to break it is the care he brings to his wife

135.reading: The girl tells her friend that her skin has lost its tender sheen, her forehead is spread with pallor like the peerkku flower, her eyes weep, and her mind is changed like Aathi Manthi's; her lover has crossed the forest where iruppai flowers fall on the rock like dice in the burning wind, and her heart that trusted him is shaken like Kazhuvul's Kamur when fourteen Velir of undying fame attacked it together.
135.nuance: Two legendary disasters frame her state: Aathi Manthi who lost her husband to the river and went mad, and the siege of Kamur by fourteen chiefs at once. Her trust (தெளிந்த) is the fortress that has fallen.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the sun-scorched forest

comparisons.tenor: the pallor on her forehead
her mind gone strange with grief
the iruppai flowers fallen on the rock
her heart that trusted him, now shaken

136.reading: The man, kept out by his wife's unyielding sulk, recalls to his heart their wedding: the feast of ghee-rich rice, the good omens and the moon in Rohini, the drums, the bathing of the bride, the arugu and vaakai garland tied with white thread, the sand-strewn pandal; and on the first night, when he asked her to loosen the cloth that made her forehead sweat and pulled the covering, her body flashed like a sword from its sheath, and not knowing how to hide she bowed her head in shame and hid in the darkness of her flowered hair.
136.nuance: This is the fullest account of a wedding in the anthology. The sulk of the colophon is not in the poem: the man answers present refusal only by remembering her first shyness, and the poem ends inside the memory.

colophon.thurai: உணர்ப்புவயின் வாராஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem gives no landscape; the colophon's sulk decides it

comparisons.tenor: the dark petals of the arugu buds
the sand strewn thick under the pandal
her body suddenly revealed

occasion.words: உணர்ப்புவயின் வாராஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

137.reading: The friend tells the girl who fears he will leave that although he has not even set out for the forest track where a tusker, longing for his mate, follows her footprints past the travellers' mud wells, her forehead has already become a waste like the empty theatre with cold hearths in the grove at the Chola's Uranthai the day after the Panguni festival, and her shoulders, once like the tall bamboo on Chezhiyan's hill, have lost their old beauty: I grieve.
137.nuance: The friend's point is the girl's haste: she wastes for a parting that has not happened. The tusker following its mate's tracks on the very road she fears quietly answers her fear.

thinai_evidence.note: the dry forest track with its mud wells

comparisons.tenor: her forehead gone waste
her shoulders in their old beauty

iraicchi.act: the tusker, longing for his mate, follows her footprints as he crosses the track
iraicchi.sense: on the road she fears he will take, even the tusker cannot be parted from his mate, so he will not leave her

138.reading: With her lover outside, the girl tells her friend that when she wept for no cause her mother suspected something else and every night, wearing neem and blue lily, with music like the Pothiyil falls of the Pandya, has Murugu brought into the house and sings of the kadamba and the elephant, searching for the cause: is that good? Her own heart thinks only of the long hard way by which the hill lord comes at midnight, over the peak where in pitch darkness a dragonfly sipping kaanthal is bewildered by the colour of a snake that has spat its jewel.
138.nuance: The mother's veriyaattu is described in full (Murugu brought into the house, the kadamba and the elephant sung) and dismissed by the girl as a vain search; aimed at the listening lover, it warns that the household is already looking for the cause.

thinai_evidence.note: the hilltop at midnight, the hour of the tryst

comparisons.tenor: the sweet music of the rite

139.reading: The wasting girl tells her friend that the rains have had their last day of darkening, flashing and roaring, the empty clouds play on the high hills at dawn, the stag has drunk and grazed and rests with his lovely mate in the pidavam shade, and red velvet-mites shine by the running water; if he still does not come, what has become of him, for was this not the thundering season in which he said he would come?
139.nuance: The landscape is all fulfilment (the rain spent, the stag at rest with its mate), so the only thing missing is the man. The last two lines can be read as 'this is not the season he named' (a comfort she tries on herself) or 'was it not this season' (the broken promise); the second fits her fear in line 17.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting through the rains for a man who promised to return with them

comparisons.tenor: the cloud darkening the sky
the lightning flashing
the thunder rising and rolling
the red velvet-mites spread by the water

iraicchi.act: the stag, fed and watered, rests at ease beside his mate in the shade
iraicchi.sense: the season has brought every creature home to its mate, so the man's absence has no excuse

140.reading: After his first meeting with her, the man tells his companion that the salt-merchant's young daughter, crying 'white salt for the same measure of paddy!' through the street with her bangles jingling, startled by a barking house dog, turned on him eyes like fighting kayal fish, and they have become a sickness that makes him strain and breathe hot like the ox yoked to her father's cart sunk in deep old mud.
140.nuance: The simile turns on her own family: the man compares himself to the beast that pulls her father's salt cart out of the mire, so his love has already yoked him to her household.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishermen's salt pans in the backwater

comparisons.tenor: her startled eyes
the deep dark mire
the man labouring in his lovesickness

links.note: Both turn on Karikalan's victories: Purananuru 66 praises the king but sets above him the defeated king at Venni who, ashamed of a wound in the back, starved himself to death; Akananuru 125 likens the fleeing north wind to the nine kings who abandoned their umbrellas on the Vaakai field.
links.teaches: Read together they show the warrior code from both sides: the loser who dies of shame earns more praise than the victor, while the losers who run are proverbial for disgrace, so an akam poet could call a wind cowardly by naming Karikalan's battle.

links.note: Both tell of Anni and Thithiyan's punnai tree: 145 has Anni felling the old punnai at the Kurukkai field, 126 has Anni, deaf to Evvi's counsel, coveting the punnai and dying in the fight.
links.teaches: The two poems give two halves of one story, the felling of the tree in 145 and the rejected counsel and death in 126, and each poet used only the half his speaker needed: a curse on the man who took a daughter, a warning to a stubborn heart.

links.note: Both name Cheralathan who drove off the sea-foe and cut the kadamba: in 127 his buried tribute is the measure of wealth the lover would refuse, in 347 the drum made after that victory is the measure of the town's loud gossip.
links.teaches: One king's campaign gave akam poets two different scales, its plunder for riches and its victory drum for noise, which shows how a puram deed was broken into separate stock comparisons.

links.note: Both are the man's words after first seeing the girl, about her eyes: the Kural says her look eats the life of those who see it; the Akananuru man tells the friends who rebuke him that they would not rebuke him if they had seen her look.
links.teaches: The Kural states the power of the look as a general truth, while the Akananuru puts it into a defence before the man's companions, showing that the couplet's claim first served as the hero's answer to rebuke (கழற்றெதிர்மறை).

links.note: Both describe the hero-stone of a man killed recovering cattle, crowned with peacock feather and inscribed with his name (பீலி சூட்டி, பெயர் பொறித்து); 264 mourns the dead man, 131 lines the road with such stones.
links.teaches: Purananuru 264 shows one stone as a single loss to the bards who depended on the man, and Akananuru 131 shows rows of them as the reason a lover will not travel, so the same memorial carried grief in puram and deterrence in akam.

links.note: In both a returning man in the rains spares mating creatures: in 4 he has tied his chariot bells so the bees paired in the flowers are not startled, in 134 he tells the charioteer to drive gently lest the stag and doe in union hear the chariot.
links.teaches: Placed side by side the two poems show a fixed mullai motif, the returning husband's gentleness toward paired creatures, that a poet could vary from bees to deer and from the man's own act to his order to the charioteer.

links.note: Both have the waiting girl say her pallor is like the peerkku flower (பீர்) and her bewilderment like Aathi Manthi's (பேதுற்று), alongside a siege simile for her state.
links.teaches: The repetition of three linked images in two poems by different poets shows that pallor, Aathi Manthi and a besieged town formed a ready set for the abandoned girl's lament.

links.note: Kazhuvul's Kamur appears in both: in 135 it is the town besieged by fourteen Velir, the image of her shaken heart; in 365 it is the place whose fragrant vengai the girl's hair recalls to the travelling man.
links.teaches: The same chieftain's town served one poet as a picture of ruin and another as a picture of fragrance, so akam poets drew on a place's whole fame, its war and its groves, and not on a single fixed meaning.

links.note: Both describe the rains that mark the promised return: in 4 the friend points to the rains to assure the girl he is coming; in 139 the rains are already over and he has not come.
links.teaches: Read in sequence the friend's argument from the season in 4 meets its test in 139, where the same signs, unanswered, turn from a promise into proof of delay.

links.note: Both are neythal poems in which the man answers his companion about a girl's eyes; in 130 she stands on Korkai's pearl-strewn harbour, in 140 she is a salt-merchant's daughter crying her wares in the street.
links.teaches: The same thurai is given to a girl of the rich harbour and to a salt-seller's daughter, and in 140 the man even compares himself to her father's ox, so the kalavu situation was open to heroines of trading families and drew its images from their work.

akananuru:123: lineation flag: the last line is numbered 12 though the poem has 14 lines.

akananuru:125: the colophon thurai begins with a stray digit (2தலைமகன்) and has தலைமகட்கச் for தலைமகட்குச்; copied as is in `colophon`. The colophon's speaker (the friend, on learning he has returned) does not fit the poem, which addresses the north wind and makes the return conditional (வல்வரின்).

akananuru:131: numbering flag: the poem is printed with the number 130.
akananuru:132: lineation flag: a printed line number 5 stands on line 10.
akananuru:140: line 12 மாமூ தள்ளல் is a sandhi split of மாமூது அள்ளல் (the old deep mire); not an error, but the word division is misleading.
